Risk Assessment in Crop Insurance using Remote Sensing Data

Abstract:

Crop yield distribution modelling plays a pivotal role in the actuarial pricing of crop insurance, with mis-pricing carrying significant economic and policy consequences. Inaccurate yield density estimation can distort premium setting, exacerbate adverse selection, and consequently destabilise insurance programmes. Such concerns have been observed in the Indian context, where pricing inefficiencies have been linked to low participation among marginalised farming communities despite higher uptake among wealthier landowners. Despite these risks, much of the existing literature relies exclusively on historical yield data, often neglecting agrometeorological variables that could improve predictive accuracy. Furthermore, while remote sensing technologies, particularly vegetation indices, offer substantial potential for enhancing risk assessment, their integration into yield distribution modelling remains limited.

This study addresses these gaps by developing a hybrid crop insurance framework that incorporates remotely sensed variables into the probabilistic estimation of yield distributions.

The objectives of the research are threefold, first, to evaluate the predictive capability of remotely sensed vegetation indices and meteorological variables in estimating wheat yield second, to identify the most appropriate statistical distribution for modelling yield in Northern India and third, to facilitate midseason forecasting of crop yield for risk assessment. For the first objective, the study employs a classical linear regression framework to quantify the relationship between crop yield and three satellite-derived vegetation indices together with temperature observations, aiming to generate yield predictions across 16 wheat-growing districts of Northern India. For the second objective, both parametric and non-parametric approaches are applied to fit yield distributions, with Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) used for risk assessment, placing particular emphasis on bandwidth selection to optimise estimator performance for each insurance unit This study extends the existing literatures by systematically evaluating bandwidth selection methods and identifying optimal parameters for KDE in the context of crop insurance. Furthermore, for the third objective the methodology incorporates midseason forecasting to enable earlier risk evaluation, supported by a Bayesian framework that facilitates dynamic updating of predictions and quantification of parameter uncertainty.

The findings indicate that integrating remote sensing variables into yield modelling enhances the explanatory and predictive capacity of crop insurance frameworks, with notable differences across three vegetation indices. While seasonal maximum value of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) during the crop period demonstrates moderate predictive capability, stronger performance is achieved when combining the average of maximum Leaf Area Index (LAI) with temperature. When employing Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FAPAR) independently of meteorological inputs it gives higher predictability. In evaluating the economic implications of model selection, the non-parametric KDE approach produced smaller discrepancies between predicted and actual monetary losses than the parametric alternatives. However, it occasionally showed sensitivity to sample variation and the choice of bandwidth. This suggests that, when appropriately calibrated, non-parametric methods can improve the precision of risk estimation and contribute to more equitable premium setting. The analysis also highlights the importance of bandwidth selection, where statistical optimisation alone is insufficient, and the modeller&rsquos judgement remains essential to achieving robust results. Further, the comparison of premiums reveals that traditional pricing methods may underestimate underlying risk, whereas the Bayesian framework captures a fuller spectrum of uncertainties.

By combining satellite-derived vegetation indices with agrometeorological variables in Bayesian and non-parametric modelling frameworks, this research improves the accuracy and timeliness of yield forecasts, which in turn allows crop insurance premiums to be priced more precisely. The methodological refinement in kernel bandwidth selection reduces errors in estimating the loss distribution. These advances not only strengthen the scientific foundation for insurance pricing design but also improve operational design through scalable, digital, and responsive insurance products that can update premiums or trigger payouts dynamically, thereby, making schemes more reliable and attractive, especially in data-scarce or climate-vulnerable regions.

Keywords: Crop Insurance, Risk Assessment, Bayesian Analysis, Actuarial premium pricing, Insurance Premium Pricing, Remote Sensing Data
